Democratic incumbent John Ossoff and Republican Congressman Mike Collins squared off on immigration
during a debate for Georgia's Senate race today.
Collins accused Ossoff of backing open borders and he touted the "Laken Riley Act," which
was named after a Georgia nurse killed by a man who was in the U.S. illegally.
Illegal immigrants, though, that John Ossoff led into this country.
Not only were coming over here killing people and murdering people like Lake and Riley,
and he wouldn't shut the door on it, human trafficking that he just let continue to flow,
but they were also taking the jobs that young people, young Americans, could go out there
and get.
Ossoff said Collins needs to answer for President Trump's deportation campaign.
They promised to go after the worst of the worst.
Instead, they've rounded up people at job sites with no suspicion of any criminal history.
They've ripped breastfeeding infants from their mothers.
They've unleashed federal agents to kill Americans on the streets of our cities with
impunity.
That's Mike Collins' immigration policy.
Ossoff began the election cycle viewed as the most vulnerable Democratic senator, but
he's vastly outraised Collins.
As Hurricane Isaias churns in the Gulf, residents in Mexico Beach on the Florida Panhandle are
thinking back to Hurricane Michael, a Category 5 storm that crushed the community eight years
ago this weekend, Randy Vuckstoe with WFSU tells us how that's impacted their preparation
for the storm.
As Isaias continues to head towards landfall, Miles Magalski, Mexico Beach city administrator,
says community members are feeling nervous.
He says in years past a hurricane may have been excused for a party, but this time...
As of Hurricane Michael now, I've not heard of one party being scheduled for this particular
Friday night.
As of now, the storm has rejected the head north, making landfall somewhere between Pensacola
and Alabama.
But many Mexico Beach residents say the path reminds them of what they saw with Michael.
Now they are preparing for the worst, setting up sandbags, grabbing supplies, and moving
vehicles to higher ground.
For NPR News, I'm Randy Vuckstoe in Panama City, Florida.
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller says he expects the central bank to raise interest
rates again to tamp down stubborn inflation.
But as NPR's Scott Horsley reports, Waller sees the timing of a rate hike as flexible.
Speaking at a conference in Istanbul organized by Turkey's central bank, Waller said inflation
in the U.S. has been too high for too long, and he's seen too little progress towards
the Fed's inflation target of 2 percent.
Waller and his colleagues at the Fed voted unanimously last month to raise their benchmark
interest rate by a quarter percentage point.
Waller says that's probably not the last rate hike that will be needed.
The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meeting, but they should be in place in an
acceptable period of time.
Investors expect the Fed to hold its benchmark interest rates steady at this month's meeting,
with an increase likely when policymakers meet in December.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Mortgage rates climbed higher for the seventh week in a row.
They're now at their highest level in nearly three years, 7.4 percent.
A year ago, the average rate was 6.3 percent.
This is NPR.
Workers for Christa Pike say she has taken her first steps with assistance one week after
a failed execution in Tennessee left her in critical condition.
She was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder.
The lethal injection drug didn't kill her, and her lawyers said her arms were left burned
and blistered.
It was Tennessee's second failed execution in four months.
UPS is hiring more than 100,000 seasonal workers for the holiday season.
As Marlon Hyde from member station WABE reports, this comes as the company cuts operational
positions and leans more on A.I.
UPS package volume can nearly double during the holidays, its peak season.
In preparation for it, the company is hiring 100,000 temporary employees nationwide to
help out.
That's fewer than in prior years as it uses more artificial intelligence.
UPS says over two-thirds of its U.S. packages are being processed through automation-equipped
buildings up from a year ago.
The company is introducing new or enhanced automated facilities in Denver, St. Paul,
Syracuse, and Portland.
Meanwhile, UPS continues to slim down by 30,000 workers this year to reduce operational costs.
For NPR News, I'm Marlon Hyde in Atlanta.
PepsiCo plans to raise prices on some stacks and drinks and slash corporate costs in the
coming weeks after posting disappointing third-quarter results.
The single-digit percentage price hikes will hit Doritos, ruffles, sun chips, and some
sodas.
The company says it needs to recoup its growing costs for fuel, aluminum, and agricultural
commodities.
I'm Rylan Barton.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
